title: Guffey Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Guffey wells have a 248 ft median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $22,100-$36,800.
h1: Guffey, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land around Guffey means planning around fractured mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow groundwater layer. Records within 5 miles show 680 permitted wells, with 485 recorded as constructed. Among wells reporting depth, the median is 248 feet, and the middle half runs from 150 to 340 feet.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and nearly all named aquifers are unnamed fractured-bedrock wells. That makes nearby well records useful, but not a guarantee for a specific lot. Lake George, Florissant, Cripple Creek, Canon City, Midland, and Victor provide useful regional context, but the closest comparable wells matter most.

sections.heading: Guffey well depth reflects fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
A Guffey driller bidding a new well will usually be working in fractured granite or gneiss. The local median depth is 248 feet. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 150 and 340 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 450 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 1,000 feet.

The depth mix shows why a single shallow estimate is risky: 53% are between 100 and 300 feet, 38% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 7% are under 100 feet. Only 2% reach 600 feet or more. For a buyer, neighboring permits can help set a drilling range, but fractured rock can change quickly across a mountain property. Ask for a bid that explains what happens if the hole must continue past the planned depth.

sections.heading: What Guffey wells usually produce
sections.html:
Of the permitted wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute, so that range is a reasonable starting point for discussing household supply, storage, and pump selection with a contractor.

Low-yield wells are present, but they are not the dominant result: 4% report under 1 gallon per minute, 20% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 68% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 8% report more than 15 gallons per minute. A well producing under 1 gallon per minute may still work with adequate storage, but it gives a buyer less margin for peak household use. Confirm the testing method and consider storage rather than judging the property from a permit number alone.

sections.heading: Guffey water levels and the measured trend
sections.html:
Only 52 wells in the records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth or permit sample. In those records, the median depth to water is 95 feet, with the middle half between 65 and 138 feet below the surface.

The decade comparison moves from a median of 92 feet below surface in the 2010s to 102 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper measured water level in the later decade, but the available measurements are limited and may not represent the same wells, seasons, or conditions. It is not enough by itself to establish a broad water-table decline. For a lot under contract, ask for the closest static-water measurements and have a driller evaluate casing, grout, pump setting, and expected drawdown.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Guffey, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across several decades. The records show 5 permits in the 1960s, 67 in the 1970s, 93 in the 1980s, 231 in the 1990s, 103 in the 2000s, 72 in the 2010s, and 57 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is not only an old-well area.

Mountain Well Improvement LLC, listed with Wiley, David D., appears most often with 178 records. Woods Drilling Inc., listed with Woods, William D., has 49, and Black Mountain Drilling, listed with Schnoes, Adam J., also has 49. Those records describe local permit history, not a guarantee of current availability, price, or workmanship. Check current licensing, references, and a written scope before selecting a driller.

sections.heading: What a new Guffey well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock and a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 248-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $16,100 to $24,800. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $22,100 to $36,800 at that median depth. A property requiring 450 feet or more could cost substantially more than the median-depth example, while a shallower hole may cost less. Get the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, pump equipment, water testing, trenching, electrical, and any difficult access charges. A permit record can help with expectations, but it does not lock in a bid.

sections.heading: Guffey risks to investigate before buying
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve attention because most permits identify unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 663 wells in that category and 9 identified as Fractured Granite. The records include 4% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, so ask how a failed or marginal hole is handled financially before work begins.

Environmental review also matters. Within about 10 miles, the map includes 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 205 historic mine features, although there are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a problem on a particular parcel. Test an existing well before closing and consider a broader water-quality review where mine workings or PFAS sites are relevant. Confirm septic setbacks, usable building area, access for drilling equipment, and the location of the well relative to the septic system.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Guffey lot
sections.html:
Start with the nearest permitted wells, not just the countywide story. Compare their depths, reported yields, static water levels, completion information, and use. The local permit mix is 94% domestic or household and 21% stock, with no irrigation or monitoring wells reported, so a buyer should verify that the existing permit supports the intended use.

For new construction, have a driller walk the site before finalizing the house location. Plan the well, septic system, driveway, electrical route, and storage together. Colorado DWR permitting and exempt household-use rules apply, and an exempt well has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. Make the purchase contract address water testing, well inspection, production testing, and the consequences of an unsuccessful hole.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Guffey, Colorado?
faq.a: Guffey wells with reported depths have a 248-foot median. The middle half runs from 150 to 340 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 450 feet. Records range from under 100 feet to a deepest reported well of 1,000 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make the depth on one parcel an imperfect predictor for the next.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Guffey?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 248-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $16,100 to $24,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $22,100 to $36,800. Access, extra depth, casing, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Guffey wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 8.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Four percent of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, while 68% are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the actual well test and plan storage around the tested production.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Guffey?
faq.a: A permit record does not establish that water is safe to drink. The area has 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 205 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new well for relevant minerals, bacteria, and other concerns before drinking it, especially near mine features.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Guffey?
faq.a: The available water-level records are limited to 52 wells. Median depth to water was 92 feet below surface in the 2010s and 102 feet in the 2020s. That later figure is deeper, but the measurements may involve different wells and conditions. The series suggests a possible change, not proof of a regionwide decline, so check nearby well data.
